description:
The AMD RX 6950 XT video card launched today. Sapphire sent an RX 6950 XT Nitro+ Pure for us to review. We're benchmarking it for power, thermals, gaming performance, and more.
Sponsor: Linode Hosting - get $100 credit with GN (https://geni.us/UaKrUmF)

We have a tear-down of the Sapphire Nitro Pure coming up!

The RX 6950 XT draws a lot of power, but it does depend (to some extent) on which partner model you buy. The Sapphire Pure that we're looking at has heavier VBIOS power consumption than the AMD official spec, putting it close to 500W when overclocked. That's a lot of headroom, but also a lot of power, and ranks it alongside some of the more OC-focused NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti GPUs, like the EVGA RTX 3090 Ti FTW3. In these benchmarks, we'll compare the Sapphire RX 6950 XT vs. the RTX 3090, RTX 3090 Ti, RX 6900 XT, and the cheaper RTX 3080 & RX 6800 XT alternatives.

We reviewed the RTX 3090 Ti here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HWS9G2WT42Q

And the original RX 6900 XT here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1ITdex_JrBM  

If you want more behind the scenes on GN check out our GN Extras side channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCgeS8J9W62B-uLBgzp14BtQ

comments.text:
I bought a Red Devil Ultimate 6900XT a few months ago and noticed it was running very hot. At stock it was over 80C and thermal throttling at 110C junction, but still boosting to 2.4GHz. I was unable to tell if this was normal boosting behavior or too hot through googling the problem, because it was within spec. An XTXH die should just boost until it runs out of power, thermals, or frequency. I undervolted it and adjusted the fan curves. Now it's running at 70C/90C at 251W.

I found out very quickly the blase attitude towards reviews while GPUs were difficult to buy translated into not very much information being available for these cards once they became available. I'm only considering, just now, after your review of a completely different 520mm2 Navi die card, that maybe I should look into RMAing my card because it's too hot.

They probably do it for compatibility, but cases that small probably won't fit a 4-slot card no matter the size of the bracket, so again, I'm happy to see it done right here. Excellent review, as always!
comments.author: @AtomicFallout757

comments.text:
I think there are pros and cons to this. There are several SFF cases that can fit large 3-slot cards, but only have 2 slot covers at the back of the case since they were only designed for mITX motherboards. Sometimes, there is room for a 3-slot bracket to overhang, sometimes not (case edges, retention mechanisms, etc).
The best solution would be to include an interchangeable slot cover for the video card, so users who can't fit a 3-slot retention bracket into their case can swap it out for a 2-slot option.
comments.author: @V_is_for_Void

comments.text: @V_is_for_Void  Perhaps this is true for the Sapphire card, but when it comes to say the EVGA RTX 3090 Ti FTW3 I would disagree seeing as that is a 4-slot card. Even though it has a 2-slot bracket, I do not know of any SFF cases that would fit that kind of card, and even if there were some, they would be bought by such a small minority that it would be much more beneficial to just put a 4-slot bracket on it in the first place. Just my opinion though.

comments.text:
3090 Ti and 3090 use the exact same die (GA-102), just with more enabled units.
You can't linearly scale CUDA cores to price, since yields are bell-shaped, so exponentially fewer cards have more functional units above a certain point. And pricing doesn't scale linearly, since the top end users will pay more for diminishing returns.
All this is not saying that I don't think the 3090 Ti is overpriced (I think it is), but rather that the economics of yield and pricing structure are not linear relations.

comments.text:
@khaledm.1476  Forcing them to be so labelled for mining would be bizarre for various reasons, while for production workloads that would just be saying they are somehow pro cards, which is not the marketing angle either company prefers. Movie studios use RTX 8000s, not gamer cards, and they don't run 24/7 (renderfarms are far more relevant in that regard). As the other poster said, there is no consistent usage for these devices, any labels would have to caveat their rating by correlating it with a particular usage; it is not useful information, people who buy these products don't read such labels and nor are they typically capable of making productive use of it in a viable manner. You must also remember that any such legal enforcement would require structures of creation, management, imposition and enforcement that would therefore itself consume resources via greater state spending (offices & buildings needed for relevant staff, paperwork, computers, databases, etc.) TCO is a vital consideration here, yet people tend to ignore the 'overhead' of any supposed eco mandate; expanding the size of the state to run such a thing just makes matters worse, it consumes more resources in the process overall, not less.

I have a 1080 Ti in an oc'd 2700K setup, it's a power hungry machine in many ways, but I generally have little time to use it (and when I do it's not for long) so the running cost is minimal, doubly so the fact that  the games I play easily max out at the 1080p TV's 60Hz, leaving the GPU running far below its max rating. In other words, just because a GPU has a particular max power consumption, that doesn't mean someone using it will typically or even ever see that usage in practice. It depends on the games they play, the resolution, settings, whether they run typical 60Hz locked or use a high refresh display, etc. Worth noting here that  the emergence of variable refresh & syncing technologies along with high refresh displays has vastly increased the potential max power draw of PCs, because in the past it just didn't matter if one was achieving silly fps numbers, one would just lock it to 60Hz and leave it at that (I stil do), and such systems when running so fast also drive the CPU, RAM, etc. harder aswell (how convenient that via physiological changes those who move to high refresh displays cannot go back, they can't undo their switch to what is an inherantly higher resource consuming means of playing games). I'm moving the GPU shortly to a 5600X setup which will cut the rest of the system draw in half and collapse the idle draw aswell, then I will tailor UV/UC profiles for each game; keep the 1080 Ti going for as long as possible is far 'greener' than buying any replacement GPU (same applies to cars and most other products, but the encouraged norm is to replace, to throw away the old, rather than make do and mend). There are other ways of dealing with power consumption issues.

Lastly, and to make matters worse IRL, there is the errant assumption that if people save money via lower power consumption it is therefore greener. This is almost always false, because the vast majority of such people then spend that saved money on more resource consumption, ie. they buy other stuff; they don't save the money, especially during times of high inflation, and it's virtually impossible for one to discern what any supposed savings are anyway because it's a comparatively small amount spread out over a long time period (some will start talking about smart meter systems and suchlike, but those devices consume resources to produce, so again the contradiction). Like I said to a friend who moaned about fuel price rises, all they need do to counter it is just not buy one of the bottles of alcoholic beverage they typically obtain every week, the saving would negate many weeks of fuel price hikes.

This is why almost all eco programmes, especially those run by state agencies, actually result in more resource consumption and more pollution, because their claimed success is generally measured by how much money they save, ignoring the fact that said money is then spent on further resource usage. Who in these comments talking about power draw and electricity prices does not on a regular basis buy things they don't need? To be genuinely green, all one need do is just not buy stuff that isn't necessary (something govts don't want people to do because mass spending sustains the state via tax take, without it many nations would have a liquidity crisis and SME debt collapse), but that's very hard for people to resist in these wasteful times. In the case of state programmes, monetary savings ought to result in a reduction of the size of govt, if such savings show that relevant structures have become larger than necessary, but that never happens, govt always expands. It's a relevant indicator that the public is now referred to as "consumers" as opposed to just potential buyers.

These issues are complex and interwoven, distorted by political spin to obtain votes, exploited by companies for marketing, misunderstood by the public because humans are rotten at understanding risk, probabilities and big picture thinking. People will sit in a 4x4 in a queue at a recycling depot with the engine running just to drop off a single bag of plastic bits (genuine example, quote from a site manager).

Other factors such as the appearance of being green in whatever manner having implications for a person's social standing (virtue signalling) make all of this even worse, eg. people who care about validation from strangers via social media, yet they'll spend thousands each year on makeup or other stuff they don't need. They buy the next shiney thing because if they keep using the old but perfectly functional thing they think they will look bad within their social circles. The nature of high end PC tech has become no less guilty of promoting such social pressures, but in the end it's the choie of the potential buyer whether to succumb to them; alas most people find it difficult to defer gratification, and in hard times it's quite understandable many will buy a new thing because they need the emotional uplift, as all around them everything else seems to be going down the crapper.

comments.text:
@cm01  Seeing this trend of increasing power is great news. Don't understand me wrong; It is not ok for people interested in these particular cards, but definitely for people interested in GPU's in the near future.

About 12 years ago we have seen the same trend; where the GTX 480 was so power hungry that it was basically running at unsafe temperatures on stock clock with insane fan rpm and noise. On AMD's side the same thing was occuring simultaneously with the HD 5970 and HD 6970. (they even had dual GPU, single PCB cards back then, thats how far they went) I remember that all GPU reviewers started to only focus on temps and noise instead of performance.

What is the similarity you might ask? 
Well it indicates that the 2 manufacturers are driving eachother to new heights. The first "cheap" gains start by slapping bigger coolers on the GPU's and increase their clocks and power draw (3090 Ti and RX 6950 XT) to simply try to outperform the competitor. Since this first step is now performed, and more performance is simply not possible with the current GPU's, the next step to win from the competitor is by increasing technology level. Therefore this competiveness between the 2 manufacturers will lead to a faster development of technology. 

Remember when AMD was lagging behind Nvidia and the step from GTX 10xx to RTX20xx kinda sucked? Thats what you get when 2 manufacturers are not competing; there was no need for NVidia to heavily invest in performance development so they just focussed on implementing some ray tracing.

Now when Intel joins this GPU race, things will get even more exiting.

Totally agree with others voicing concern on power draw. But I want you guys to remember that you can under volt and under clock your cards to use less power by using programs like MSI afterburner. Just have an ecomony mode set for normal use and full mode when needed. Yes doing so requires a little will power. Keep in mind often you will save power by under clocking a stronger tier card as it has to work less. While the lower tier card needs more power to run properly. So its mostly simple to clock your card to a lower tier card rating and get that same performance of the lower tier card while using less power.

Just sharing a helpful tip so your options are less limiting. In my opinion, the 600-800 power watt usage of the 4000 series cards are just way too power hungry for an average home. Better to buy current gen cheaper in the future or skip next gen for the more future energy optomized versions that follow.

comments.text: I don't really know whether the 6950XT uses the XTX or the XTXH die (latter is higher leakage, higher clocking, but both are the same hardware), but if it's the former, their cores should pretty much perform identically on average, accounting for silicon lottery and such. If it's the latter, the 6950XT should consistently clock higher than the 6900XT. Regardless, the one thing the 6900XT can't match it in is memory. The best memory overclocking 6900XTs barely even reach 2250MHz, which is the stock speed for the 6950XT. If we assume that a 6950XT's memory can overclock about as much, then we're talking about 2400MHz memory, or about 19.2Gbps. That's a hefty increase and should account for quite a bit of performance difference. Now, if it's also an XTXH die, the combined added overclocking potential should be quite a big one. But even so, it's only for benchmarking and maybe some 4K games. For normal use, the differences will be negligible, as they already are when you go with anything above a 6800XT/3080.

comments.text:
@Linkedblade  Nah, the cooling isn't actually the expensive part, since most cards use the same design(talking AIBs here) just scaled up, the actual costs are very low, cause the designing part is usually the most costly. They aren't making these coolers in the US or Europe where human labour is expensive, these get made in China or Taiwan, or in China, but actually North Korea(yeah Chinese companies out-source a ton of factory work to North Korea, but pretend it's made in China to export it legally)  so costs of manufacturing are quite low. Material costs aren't that bad either, the copper heatpipes would be the most expensive part, but not even that bad per card basis, I would be very surprised if a cooler costs over 100 Euro to produce, it's likely to be much lower then that, remember these aren't custom made products, but factory line mass produced products meaning the costs of components drop due to economies of scale.

It's in fact mostly the silicon costs that are driving these prices, next to having to make the investors happy with a good return on investment through profit margins and better stock prices. 

Many people don't realize that with newer nodes the price per wafer is not uncommon to be over triple if not quadruple or more the cost of the wafers of the previous node. Combine that with higher power draws, leading to much more suficticated board designs, requiring higher quality designs of power delivery(still not a big costs compared to silicon btw, power delivery components on such a scale of purchase won't be more then a dollar or 2 per individual VRM component)

a 10nm wafer can easily cost 6000 Dollars, with 7nm close to 10000 dollars, with 5nm costing around 17000 dollars. The prices are increasing with each node exponentially instead of linearly.
